title: Chapter XXVIII

teacherSummary.text: Arriving at Hunsford, Elizabeth is shown every room and the garden by Collins, who praises Lady Catherine constantly. Charlotte manages him skillfully and keeps her own sitting room. They glimpse Lady Catherine's sickly daughter, Anne.

vocabulary.definition: The state or quality of being neat
vocabulary.context: It was rather small, but well built and convenient; and everything was fitted up and arranged with a neatness and consistency of which Elizabeth gave Charlotte all the credit.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “neatness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A piece of dining-room furniture having compartments and shelves for keeping or displaying articles of table service
vocabulary.context: After sitting long enough to admire every article of furniture in the room, from the sideboard to the fender, to give an account of their journey and of all that had happened in London, Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sideboard”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Collins and Charlotte were both standing at the gate in conversation with the ladies; and Sir William, to Elizabeth’s high diversion, was stationed in the doorway, in earnest contemplation of the greatness before him, and constantly bowing whenever Miss de Bourgh looked that way.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “station”: -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Inclining or inclined from the plane of the horizon, or from a horizontal or other right line
vocabulary.context: The garden sloping to the road, the house standing in it, the green pales and the laurel hedge, everything declared they were arriving.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sloping”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of standing or adhering together, or being fixed in union, as the parts of a body
vocabulary.context: It was rather small, but well built and convenient; and everything was fitted up and arranged with a neatness and consistency of which Elizabeth gave Charlotte all the credit.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “consistency”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + sist (Latin sistere, "to stand"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A yielding of judgment or preference from respect to the wishes or opinion of another
vocabulary.context: She is the sort of woman whom one cannot regard with too much deference.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deference”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of turning aside from any course, occupation, or object
vocabulary.context: Collins and Charlotte were both standing at the gate in conversation with the ladies; and Sir William, to Elizabeth’s high diversion, was stationed in the doorway, in earnest contemplation of the greatness before him, and constantly bowing whenever Miss de Bourgh looked that way.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “diversion”: -sion (Latin -sio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I have scarcely any hesitation in saying that she will include you and my sister Maria in every invitation with which she honours us during your stay here.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “include”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state of society in which the relations and duties of a citizen are recognized and obeyed
vocabulary.context: She saw instantly that her cousin’s manners were not altered by his marriage; his formal civility was just what it had been, and he detained her some minutes at the gate to hear and satisfy his enquiries after all her family.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “civility”: civ (Latin civis, "citizen") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To address with expressions of sympathetic pleasure on account of some happy event affecting the person addressed
vocabulary.context: Collins no sooner saw the two girls than he began to congratulate them on their good fortune, which Charlotte explained by letting them know that the whole party was asked to dine at Rosings the next day.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “congratulate”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Rosings Park in Kent represents aristocratic wealth and patronage.

significance: Charlotte has built a contented life by managing her husband's absurdity.
discussionQuestions: How has Charlotte made her marriage work?
Where does setting appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXVIII,” how does Austen show visit to Hunsford? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXVIII develops the idea of visit to Hunsford. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses setting in Chapter XXVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of visit to Hunsford. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of visit to Hunsford responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of visit to Hunsford. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: From his garden, Mr. Collins would have led them round his two meadows, but the ladies not having shoes to encounter the remains of a white frost, turned back; and while Sir William accompanied him, Charlotte took her sister and friend over the house, extremely well pleased, probably, to have the opportunity of showing it without her husband’s help. It was rather small, but well built and convenient; and everything was fitted up and arranged with a neatness and consistency of which Elizabeth gave Charlotte all the credit. When Mr. Collins could be forgotten, there was really a great air of comfort throughout, and by Charlotte’s evident enjoyment of it, Elizabeth supposed he must be often forgotten.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXVIII”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How has Charlotte made her marriage work? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are neatness, sideboard, stationed, sloping, consistency. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “It was rather small, but well built and convenient; and everything was fitted up and arranged with a neatness and consistency of which Elizabeth gave Charlotte all the credit.” Webster's says: The state or quality of being neat. Now the word history: “neatness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “sideboard”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “station”: -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Rosings Park in Kent represents aristocratic wealth and patronage. Why does this chapter matter? Charlotte has built a contented life by managing her husband's absurdity. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for setting.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see setting, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to visit to Hunsford.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Setting, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of setting. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
